sections.title: Taxonomy and cap
sections.text: Russula rhodopus Zvára is a brittlegill in the family Russulaceae (Basidiomycota); Russula rhodopoda has been published as a synonym. The cap is generally 4–9 cm wide: convex at first, it expands and then becomes shallowly depressed in the centre. It is typically glossy blood-red to cherry-red, often darker, sometimes nearly black, at the disc. The surface remains polished-looking and may become slimy in wet weather. The margin stays smooth for a long time, becoming briefly striate at maturity.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are moderately crowded, rather thick and brittle, sometimes forked; they are whitish at first, then cream to pale ochre, and attach near the stem from narrowly adnate to almost free. The cylindrical to slightly club-shaped stem is about 4–8 × 1–2.5 cm. It is usually flushed pink or red, sometimes on one side only, rarely entirely white; it is solid when young, then spongy, and may yellow at the base with age. The flesh is white, reddish beneath the cap cuticle, brittle and may yellow with age or after injury. The spore print ranges from cream to ochre; spores are broadly ellipsoid, about 7–10 × 6.5–8 µm, with low ornamentation forming an incomplete network.

sections.title: Ecology and similar species
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal brittlegill occurs mainly in humid, acidic conifer forests, especially under spruce, sometimes among sphagnum, at middle to higher elevations. Fruiting is reported from summer into autumn, often July to October in Central European descriptions. Its combination of a glossy red cap, pinkish stem and humid-forest habitat can guide identification but is not sufficient by itself. It may be confused with other red russulas, including Russula sanguinaria, R. helodes or R. paludosa; habitat, chemical reactions and microscopy may be needed for reliable identification.

sections.title: Caution
sections.text: The Czech Mycological Society classifies this species as inedible; other field guides also advise against eating it, including because of its acrid taste. Do not taste a mushroom to identify it or eat one based on a profile or photograph. The characters summarized here do not replace a full mycological identification.

traits: Brittlegill in the family Russulaceae; Russula rhodopoda is a reported taxonomic synonym
Cap 4–9 cm wide, blood-red to cherry-red and glossy, usually darker at the centre and shallowly depressed at maturity
Moderately crowded, thick brittle gills, whitish then cream to pale ochre, sometimes forked
Stem 4–8 × 1–2.5 cm, usually flushed pink to red, sometimes on one side only, rarely white
White brittle flesh, reddish beneath the cap cuticle, liable to yellow with age or after injury
Cream to ochre spore print; broadly ellipsoid spores with low ornamentation forming an incomplete network
Ectomycorrhizal with conifers, especially spruce, in humid forests and acidic soils; classified as inedible by the Czech Myko Atlas
safetyNote: Do not taste or eat a russula identified from this profile or a photograph. The Czech Mycological Society Myko Atlas classifies Russula rhodopus as inedible. Reliable identification may require microscopic and chemical examination.
